Falsification with negative-control outcomes

Source: R/falsctl.R
falsctl.Rd

Estimates the "effect" of the treatment on outcomes it cannot have affected (negative controls: an outcome measured before treatment, or one with no plausible path from it), by the same regression as the outcome of interest. An association with a negative control points to confounding or another bias that the adjustment did not remove (Lipsitch, Tchetgen Tchetgen and Cohen 2010; Shi, Miao and Tchetgen Tchetgen 2020).

Usage

falsctl(
  data,
  y = NULL,
  d,
  nc,
  x = NULL,
  se = c("hc1", "iid"),
  nperm = 0,
  adj = c("holm", "bonferroni", "hochberg", "BH", "BY", "none"),
  alpha = 0.05,
  level = 0.95,
  seed = NULL
)

# S3 method for class 'falsctl'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

data

A data frame, one row per unit.

y

NULL or the name of the outcome of interest (numbers).

d

The name of the treatment column (numbers; it must vary).

nc

The names of the negative-control outcome columns (numbers).

x

NULL or the names of the covariate columns (numbers); for print(), an object of class falsctl.

se

"hc1" or "iid".

nperm

The permutations: a whole number from 0 (none) to 1000000.

adj

The adjustment of the controls' p-values: "holm", "bonferroni", "hochberg", "BH", "BY" or "none".

alpha

The level at which a control is flagged: one number strictly between 0 and 1.

level

The level of the intervals: one number strictly between 0 and 1.

seed

NULL (drawn from R's generator, so set.seed() fixes it) or a whole number from 0 to 2147483647; not used without permutations.

...

Not used by print().

Value

An object of class falsctl, a list: tab, a data frame with one row per outcome (outcome, role, primary or control, est, se, stat, p, lo, hi, pperm, padj; NA where not computed); nflag; ncontrol; and se, adj, alpha, level, nperm, seed (NA without permutations).

Details

Each outcome is regressed on an intercept, the covariates x and the treatment d by least squares; est is the coefficient of d with a classical (se = "iid") or HC1 ("hc1") standard error, Student's t on the residual degrees of freedom and its interval at level. With nperm > 0 each outcome also has the permutation p-value of Kennedy (1995): the residuals of the outcome on the covariates are permuted against those of d, one permutation of the rows for every outcome, pperm = (1 + k) / (1 + nperm). The controls' p-values (the permutation ones when drawn) are adjusted for their number by adj (the methods of p.adjust()); nflag counts the controls whose adjusted p-value is at most alpha.

References

Lipsitch, M., Tchetgen Tchetgen, E. and Cohen, T. (2010). Negative controls: a tool for detecting confounding and bias in observational studies. Epidemiology, 21(3), 383-388. doi:10.1097/EDE.0b013e3181d61eeb

Shi, X., Miao, W. and Tchetgen Tchetgen, E. (2020). A selective review of negative control methods in epidemiology. Current Epidemiology Reports, 7(4), 190-202. doi:10.1007/s40471-020-00243-4

Kennedy, P. E. (1995). Randomization tests in econometrics. Journal of Business and Economic Statistics, 13(1), 85-94. doi:10.1080/07350015.1995.10524581

Examples

set.seed(5)
n <- 300
d <- data.frame(age = runif(n, 18, 60), u = rnorm(n))
d$t <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(0.8 * d$u))
d$arrest <- 0.4 * d$t + 0.5 * d$u + rnorm(n)
d$prior <- 0.5 * d$u + rnorm(n)     # before treatment: a control
d$height <- rnorm(n)                # no path from treatment
falsctl(d, "arrest", "t", c("prior", "height"), x = "age")
#> falsctl: 1 of 2 negative control(s) associated with the treatment at alpha 0.05 (holm)
#>  outcome    role     est     se   stat         p      lo       hi pperm
#>   arrest primary  0.8024 0.1308  6.134 2.730e-09  0.5450 1.059832    NA
#>    prior control  0.3816 0.1282  2.976 3.159e-03  0.1293 0.633989    NA
#>   height control -0.2236 0.1171 -1.909 5.720e-02 -0.4541 0.006887    NA
#>      padj
#>        NA
#>  0.006318
#>  0.057202
